analysis.one_liner: Provides free or low-cost child care for children under six and raises child care worker pay.
analysis.headline: Referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on July 15, 2025 with 107 Democratic cosponsors; no hearing or vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a federal guarantee that every child under six in a participating state can get child care help. Families at or below 85% of their state's median income would pay nothing, and no family would pay more than 7% of its income in copays. The federal government would also pay providers rates designed to cover the real cost of care, including wages for child care workers comparable to what elementary teachers with similar credentials earn.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children under six — especially low- and middle-income families — would see their child care bills fall to zero or a small capped share of income. Child care workers would get a guaranteed living wage and pay parity with elementary educators. Child care providers would get steady public funding that covers their full operating costs, plus startup, quality, and facilities grants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with young children and child care workers

how_it_helps.text: Starting October 1, 2026, every eligible child under six in a state with an approved plan would be entitled to child care assistance, on demand rather than through waiting lists.
Families with incomes at or below 85% of their state median would pay no copayment at all; above that, copays slide up to a maximum of 7% of family income.

States must set provider payment rates high enough to cover the full cost of care, including a living wage for all staff and pay equivalent to elementary educators with similar credentials and experience, adjusted annually for inflation.
Providers receiving funds are barred from charging a family more than the subsidy plus the family's copay, so savings pass through to parents.
States would hand out startup, quality, and facilities grants to expand the number of child care slots, with priority for underserved communities.
In states that do not sign on, the bill appropriates $20 billion for grants to cities and counties and for Head Start expansion instead.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the program through mandatory appropriations described as 'such sums as may be necessary' for fiscal years 2026 through 2031 — an open-ended commitment with no capped total — plus the $20 billion and $1.3 billion appropriated for 2026. States would also have to maintain their existing child care spending and cover 10% of direct service costs and half of administrative costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, plus a state funding match

drawbacks.text: The main child care appropriation is open-ended — 'such sums as may be necessary' each year through 2031 — so the total federal cost is not capped by the bill's text and would be set by however many families enroll.

The guarantee only applies in states that submit and win approval of a state plan; families in states that opt out would be left to a much smaller pool of $20 billion in locality grants and Head Start awards, so help would be uneven across the country.

States must maintain their own child care spending at its three-year average and pay a 10% share of direct service costs and 50% of administration, which could strain state budgets and give states a reason to decline to participate.

The wage and quality requirements — payment rates covering full costs, a tiered quality system, and a licensing pathway — raise the bar for providers, and small home-based providers could face real costs in meeting them, though the bill funds startup, licensure, and facilities support to help them comply.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to families is large and direct: child care is one of the biggest household bills for parents of young children, and the bill would cut it to zero or a small capped share for most of them, while raising the pay of a workforce that is among the lowest-paid in the country. The honest objections are about scale and design: the price tag is open-ended and would depend on enrollment, the guarantee depends on each state choosing to participate, and states must chip in their own money to get federal funds. Whether it is a bargain depends on whether one accepts a major permanent federal program in exchange for a major household cost disappearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 15, 2025 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, which is the only action recorded so far.
107 House Democrats have signed on as cosponsors; the cosponsor list includes no Republicans.
The bill has not been scheduled for a committee hearing or markup, and no further action appears in its history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet; the bill has not moved, so families continue to pay today's child care prices and providers and workers are unchanged. The people best positioned under the status quo are members of the House majority, who face no vote on the bill at all.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; child care costs are unchanged

for.name: Rep. Bobby Scott
for.role: Sponsor, House Education and Workforce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 15, 2025 and assembled an initial group of roughly 80 Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 15, 2025 and has taken no further action on it.

against.name: Burgess Owens
against.role: Chair, House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill since it was referred; no committee action appears in the bill's history.

sides.party_line_note: All 107 cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on; the committee that would act on the bill has a Republican majority, so support so far runs entirely along party lines.

industries.industry: Child care providers (centers and family child care homes)
industries.note: The bill routes all federal child care assistance through these providers, guaranteeing them payment rates that cover their full operating costs plus startup, quality, and facilities grants — locking them in as the permanent channel for public child care money. Their interest lines up with families' here because the bill also bars them from charging parents more than the subsidy plus a small copay.

industries.industry: Early childhood educators and child care staff
industries.note: Payment rates must fund a living wage for all staff and pay equivalent to elementary educators with similar credentials, plus training, degree attainment, and apprenticeship support — a direct raise for one of the lowest-paid workforces in the country.

States gain a large infusion of federal child care funding (the federal government would cover 90% of direct service costs) but must maintain their own spending at prior levels and pay a 10% match for services and half of administrative costs, and they take on new planning and enforcement duties.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and a Republican-run committee that has taken no action, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or a floor vote this Congress. Its realistic path is to sit in committee — as it currently stands — and function as a statement of priorities for its cosponsors, unless control of the House or the committee's agenda changes.
